Que.q: Q1 : What are static blocks and static initializers in Java?
Que.a: Static blocks, also known as static initializers, are special blocks of code used to initialize static variables in a class. They execute automatically when the class is loaded into memory by the JVM, before any object is created or constructors are called. A class can contain multiple static blocks, and they execute in the order they appear in the source code. Static blocks are commonly used for complex initialization tasks that cannot be performed with a single assignment statement.

Que.note: Static blocks execute only once when the class is loaded by the JVM.

Que.q: Q2 : How to call one constructor from another constructor?
Que.a: In Java, one constructor can call another constructor within the same class using the this() keyword. This technique is known as constructor chaining and helps avoid code duplication. The this() call must always be the first statement inside the constructor. Depending on the arguments passed, Java selects the appropriate constructor. Constructor chaining improves code readability and maintainability by centralizing initialization logic in a single place rather than repeating it across multiple constructors.

list.1: Must be the first statement in constructor
list.2: Only one this() call is allowed in a constructor

Que.q: Q3 : What is method overriding in Java?
Que.a: Method overriding occurs when a subclass provides its own implementation of a method that already exists in its superclass with the same name, parameters, and return type. It allows runtime polymorphism and enables subclasses to define specific behavior while maintaining the same method signature. When an overridden method is called using a subclass object, the subclass version executes instead of the superclass version. Method overriding is widely used to achieve flexibility, extensibility, and dynamic behavior in object-oriented programming.

Que.note: Method overriding is used to achieve runtime polymorphism in Java.

Que.q: Q4 : What is super keyword in Java?
Que.a: The super keyword is used to access members of the immediate superclass, including variables, methods, and constructors. It is especially useful when subclass members override superclass members. By using super, a subclass can explicitly refer to the hidden or overridden members of its parent class. The super() constructor call must be the first statement in a constructor. This keyword helps maintain inheritance relationships and allows subclasses to reuse functionality defined in their parent classes.

Que.q: Q5 : Difference between method overloading and method overriding in Java?
Que.a: Method overloading and method overriding are important concepts in Java polymorphism. Overloading occurs within the same class and involves methods having the same name but different parameter lists. Overriding occurs between a superclass and subclass where methods have the same signature. Overloading supports compile-time polymorphism, while overriding supports runtime polymorphism. Overloading improves code readability by using a common method name for related operations, whereas overriding allows subclasses to provide specialized implementations of inherited methods.

Que.q: Q6 : What is an interface in Java?
Que.a: An interface in Java is a blueprint of a class that contains abstract methods and constants. It is used to achieve abstraction and multiple inheritance because a class can implement multiple interfaces. Interfaces define what a class should do rather than how it should do it. From Java 8 onwards, interfaces can also contain default and static methods. They are commonly used to establish contracts between classes and promote loose coupling, flexibility, and maintainability in object-oriented applications.

Que.note: Interfaces help achieve abstraction and multiple inheritance in Java.

Que.q: Q7 : Difference between abstract class and interface?
Que.a: Abstract classes and interfaces are both used for abstraction in Java, but they serve different purposes. An abstract class can contain both abstract and concrete methods, instance variables, and constructors. An interface primarily defines a contract that implementing classes must follow. A class can extend only one abstract class but can implement multiple interfaces. Interfaces are ideal for defining capabilities, while abstract classes are suitable when common functionality needs to be shared among related classes.

Que.q: Q8 : What is encapsulation in Java?
Que.a: Encapsulation is one of the fundamental principles of object-oriented programming that involves wrapping data and methods into a single unit called a class. It restricts direct access to an object's internal data and allows access only through public methods such as getters and setters. Encapsulation improves security, data integrity, and maintainability by controlling how data is accessed and modified. It also helps achieve loose coupling and makes applications easier to update without affecting other parts of the system.

Que.note: Encapsulation protects data by restricting direct access to class fields.

Que.q: Q9 : What is polymorphism in Java?
Que.a: Polymorphism means 'many forms' and allows a single interface or method to behave differently depending on the object involved. In Java, polymorphism is achieved through method overloading and method overriding. Compile-time polymorphism is implemented using overloading, while runtime polymorphism is achieved through overriding. Polymorphism increases flexibility, promotes code reusability, and simplifies application design. It allows developers to write generic code that can work with different object types without needing separate implementations for each type.

Que.note: Polymorphism allows one interface to represent multiple behaviors.

Que.q: Q10 : What is inheritance in Java?
Que.a: Inheritance is an object-oriented programming concept that allows one class to acquire the properties and behaviors of another class. The class that inherits is called the subclass, while the class being inherited is called the superclass. Inheritance promotes code reusability, reduces duplication, and establishes relationships between classes. Java supports single, multilevel, and hierarchical inheritance through classes, while multiple inheritance is achieved using interfaces. It is one of the core pillars of object-oriented design and application development.

Que.q: Q11 : What is a package in Java?
Que.a: A package in Java is a namespace used to organize related classes, interfaces, enums, and sub-packages. It helps avoid naming conflicts and improves code maintainability by grouping logically related components together. Packages also provide access protection and make large applications easier to manage. Java provides built-in packages such as java.lang, java.util, and java.io, while developers can create custom packages. Using packages promotes modular programming and enhances code reusability across different projects and applications.

Que.code: package com.company.employee;

Que.note: Packages help organize Java classes and prevent naming conflicts.

Que.q: Q12 : What are access modifiers in Java?
Que.a: Access modifiers in Java control the visibility and accessibility of classes, methods, variables, and constructors. They help implement encapsulation by restricting access to program components. Java provides four access modifiers: public, protected, default, and private. Public members are accessible everywhere, protected members are accessible within the package and subclasses, default members are accessible only within the package, and private members are accessible only within the same class. Proper use of access modifiers improves security and maintainability.

Que.q: Q13 : What is the difference between == and equals() in Java?
Que.a: The == operator and equals() method are both used for comparison in Java, but they work differently. The == operator compares object references and checks whether two references point to the same memory location. The equals() method compares the actual content or state of objects. For primitive data types, == compares values directly. For objects, equals() should be used when logical equality is required. Many Java classes such as String override equals() to compare object contents rather than memory addresses.

Que.note: Use equals() when comparing the contents of objects.

Que.q: Q14 : What is the difference between String, StringBuffer, and StringBuilder?
Que.a: String, StringBuffer, and StringBuilder are classes used to handle text in Java. String objects are immutable, meaning their values cannot be changed after creation. StringBuffer is mutable and thread-safe because its methods are synchronized. StringBuilder is also mutable but is not synchronized, making it faster than StringBuffer in single-threaded environments. Developers use String for constant text, StringBuffer in multi-threaded applications, and StringBuilder when high-performance string manipulation is required without thread safety concerns.

Que.q: Q15 : What is an exception in Java?
Que.a: An exception in Java is an event that disrupts the normal flow of program execution. Exceptions occur due to errors such as invalid input, file access issues, arithmetic errors, or network failures. Java provides a robust exception handling mechanism using try, catch, finally, throw, and throws keywords. Proper exception handling improves application reliability and prevents abrupt program termination. Exceptions are categorized into checked exceptions, unchecked exceptions, and errors, each serving different purposes in error management and recovery.

Que.q: Q16 : What is the difference between checked and unchecked exceptions?
Que.a: Checked and unchecked exceptions are two categories of exceptions in Java. Checked exceptions are checked at compile time and must be handled using try-catch blocks or declared with the throws keyword. Examples include IOException and SQLException. Unchecked exceptions occur at runtime and do not require explicit handling. They are subclasses of RuntimeException, such as NullPointerException and ArithmeticException. Checked exceptions usually represent recoverable conditions, while unchecked exceptions generally indicate programming errors that should be fixed in the code.

Que.q: Q17 : What is the final keyword in Java?
Que.a: The final keyword in Java is used to restrict modification. When applied to a variable, it makes the variable constant and prevents reassignment. When applied to a method, it prevents method overriding in subclasses. When applied to a class, it prevents inheritance. The final keyword is commonly used to enforce immutability, protect important functionality, and improve code reliability. It helps developers define components that should remain unchanged throughout the execution of a program.

Que.code: final int MAX_VALUE = 100;

Que.q: Q18 : What is the finally block in Java?
Que.a: The finally block is used in exception handling to execute important code regardless of whether an exception occurs or not. It is typically used for resource cleanup activities such as closing files, database connections, or network streams. The finally block executes after the try and catch blocks, even if an exception is thrown or handled. This ensures that critical cleanup operations are performed consistently. Using finally helps prevent resource leaks and improves application stability and reliability.

Que.note: The finally block executes whether an exception occurs or not.

Que.q: Q19 : What is the difference between throw and throws in Java?
Que.a: The throw keyword is used to explicitly create and throw an exception within a method or block of code. The throws keyword is used in a method declaration to indicate that the method may throw one or more exceptions. Throw is followed by an exception object, whereas throws is followed by exception class names. Together, they help manage exception propagation and error handling in Java applications. Proper use of throw and throws improves code readability and error management.

Que.q: Q20 : What is multithreading in Java?
Que.a: Multithreading is a feature in Java that allows multiple threads to execute concurrently within a single program. A thread is the smallest unit of execution, and multiple threads can run simultaneously to improve performance and responsiveness. Multithreading is commonly used in applications that perform background processing, network communication, or user interface updates. Java provides built-in support for multithreading through the Thread class and Runnable interface. Proper thread management helps maximize CPU utilization and improve overall application efficiency.

Que.q: Q21 : What is the difference between Thread and Runnable in Java?
Que.a: Thread and Runnable are two ways to create threads in Java. The Thread class provides built-in methods for thread management and can be extended to create a thread. Runnable is an interface that contains only the run() method and allows a class to implement it. Implementing Runnable is generally preferred because Java does not support multiple inheritance, allowing a class to extend another class while still creating threads. Runnable also promotes better design and code flexibility.

Que.q: Q22 : What is synchronization in Java?
Que.a: Synchronization is a mechanism in Java used to control access to shared resources by multiple threads. It prevents race conditions and ensures that only one thread can execute a synchronized block or method at a time. Synchronization helps maintain data consistency and thread safety in multithreaded applications. Java provides synchronized methods, synchronized blocks, and locks to manage concurrent access. Proper synchronization is essential when multiple threads read and modify shared data simultaneously.

Que.note: Synchronization prevents multiple threads from accessing critical code simultaneously.

Que.q: Q23 : What is a deadlock in Java?
Que.a: A deadlock is a situation in which two or more threads are permanently blocked because each thread is waiting for a resource held by another thread. As a result, none of the threads can continue execution. Deadlocks commonly occur when threads acquire locks in different orders. They can cause application hangs and performance issues. Developers can prevent deadlocks by maintaining consistent lock ordering, minimizing lock usage, and using advanced concurrency utilities provided by the Java platform.

Que.code:
Thread A waits for Lock B
Thread B waits for Lock A

Que.note: Deadlocks can stop application execution if not handled properly.

Que.q: Q24 : What is the difference between HashMap and Hashtable?
Que.a: HashMap and Hashtable are both used to store key-value pairs in Java, but they differ in several ways. HashMap is not synchronized and is therefore faster in single-threaded environments. Hashtable is synchronized and thread-safe but generally slower due to synchronization overhead. HashMap allows one null key and multiple null values, whereas Hashtable does not allow null keys or values. In modern Java applications, HashMap is preferred, while ConcurrentHashMap is often used for thread-safe operations.

Que.q: Q25 : What is the difference between ArrayList and LinkedList?
Que.a: ArrayList and LinkedList are implementations of the List interface in Java. ArrayList uses a dynamic array internally, making it efficient for random access operations. LinkedList uses a doubly linked list structure, making insertions and deletions more efficient at specific positions. ArrayList generally provides better performance for searching and retrieving elements, while LinkedList performs better when frequent modifications are required. The choice between them depends on application requirements and the type of operations performed most often.

Que.q: Q26 : What is the difference between HashSet and TreeSet?
Que.a: HashSet and TreeSet are implementations of the Set interface in Java. HashSet stores elements using a hash table and does not maintain any specific order. It provides faster performance for basic operations such as add, remove, and search. TreeSet stores elements in a sorted order using a Red-Black Tree structure. While TreeSet maintains natural ordering, it is generally slower than HashSet. The choice depends on whether ordering or performance is the primary requirement in the application.

Que.q: Q27 : What is the difference between Iterator and ListIterator?
Que.a: Iterator and ListIterator are interfaces used to traverse collections in Java. Iterator can be used with all collection types and supports forward traversal only. ListIterator is available only for List implementations and supports both forward and backward traversal. Additionally, ListIterator allows adding, updating, and replacing elements during iteration, while Iterator mainly supports element removal. ListIterator provides more functionality and flexibility when working specifically with list-based collections such as ArrayList and LinkedList.

Que.q: Q28 : What is the Java Collection Framework?
Que.a: The Java Collection Framework is a unified architecture that provides interfaces, classes, and algorithms for storing and manipulating groups of objects. It includes interfaces such as List, Set, Queue, and Map, along with implementations like ArrayList, LinkedList, HashSet, TreeSet, and HashMap. The framework offers reusable data structures, improves productivity, and simplifies application development. It also provides utility methods for sorting, searching, and synchronization. The Collection Framework is one of the most widely used components of the Java platform.

Que.note: The Collection Framework provides ready-to-use data structures and algorithms.

Que.q: Q29 : What is Comparable and Comparator in Java?
Que.a: Comparable and Comparator are interfaces used for sorting objects in Java. Comparable provides a natural ordering by implementing the compareTo() method within the class itself. Comparator allows custom sorting logic by implementing the compare() method in a separate class. Comparable is suitable when a single sorting order is sufficient, while Comparator is useful when multiple sorting criteria are needed. Both interfaces are commonly used with collections such as ArrayList and TreeSet to arrange objects in a desired order.

Que.q: Q30 : What is serialization in Java?
Que.a: Serialization is the process of converting a Java object into a byte stream so that it can be stored in a file, transferred over a network, or persisted for later use. Deserialization is the reverse process of converting the byte stream back into an object. To make a class serializable, it must implement the Serializable interface. Serialization is commonly used in distributed systems, caching mechanisms, and object persistence. It allows objects to maintain their state across different environments and program executions.

Que.note: Serialization converts objects into byte streams for storage or transmission.

Que.q: Q31 : What is transient keyword in Java?
Que.a: The transient keyword is used to indicate that a variable should not be serialized when an object is converted into a byte stream. During serialization, transient variables are ignored and their values are not saved. When the object is deserialized, transient variables receive default values based on their data types. This keyword is commonly used for sensitive information such as passwords, temporary data, or fields that can be recalculated. Using transient helps improve security and reduces unnecessary storage requirements during serialization.

Que.note: Transient fields are skipped during serialization.

Que.q: Q32 : What is the difference between serialization and deserialization?
Que.a: Serialization is the process of converting a Java object into a byte stream so it can be stored or transmitted. Deserialization is the reverse process where the byte stream is converted back into a Java object. Serialization helps preserve object state across different environments and executions. Deserialization reconstructs the original object from the stored data. Both processes are essential in distributed systems, file storage, caching, and network communication where object data needs to be transferred between applications or systems.

Que.q: Q33 : What is JVM in Java?
Que.a: JVM, or Java Virtual Machine, is a runtime environment responsible for executing Java bytecode. It acts as an intermediary between Java programs and the underlying operating system, making Java platform-independent. The JVM loads classes, verifies bytecode, manages memory, performs garbage collection, and executes code. It enables the principle of 'Write Once, Run Anywhere' by allowing the same compiled Java program to run on different operating systems. JVM is a key component of the Java ecosystem and application execution process.

Que.note: JVM executes Java bytecode and provides platform independence.

Que.q: Q34 : What is JDK, JRE, and JVM?
Que.a: JDK, JRE, and JVM are core components of the Java platform. JVM executes Java bytecode and provides the runtime environment. JRE, or Java Runtime Environment, contains the JVM along with libraries required to run Java applications. JDK, or Java Development Kit, includes the JRE and development tools such as the compiler, debugger, and documentation utilities. Developers use the JDK to create Java applications, while the JRE is used to run them. Together they form the complete Java ecosystem.

Que.q: Q35 : What is garbage collection in Java?
Que.a: Garbage collection is an automatic memory management process in Java that removes objects that are no longer reachable or used by the application. The JVM periodically identifies unused objects and frees their memory, reducing memory leaks and simplifying development. Developers do not need to manually allocate and deallocate memory as in some other programming languages. Garbage collection improves application stability, efficiency, and reliability. Various garbage collection algorithms are available in modern JVM implementations to optimize performance for different workloads.

Que.code: System.gc();

Que.note: Garbage collection automatically frees memory occupied by unused objects.

Que.q: Q36 : What is the difference between Heap and Stack memory in Java?
Que.a: Heap and Stack are two important memory areas managed by the JVM. Heap memory is used for storing objects and instance variables, while Stack memory stores method calls, local variables, and references. Heap memory is shared among all threads, whereas each thread has its own Stack memory. Objects created using the new keyword are stored in the Heap. Stack memory is automatically released when method execution completes, while Heap memory is managed through garbage collection.

Que.q: Q37 : What is immutable class in Java?
Que.a: An immutable class is a class whose objects cannot be modified after creation. Once an object is initialized, its state remains unchanged throughout its lifetime. To create an immutable class, fields should be private and final, setters should not be provided, and mutable objects should be handled carefully. The String class is a common example of an immutable class in Java. Immutable objects are thread-safe, secure, and easier to manage because their state cannot change unexpectedly after creation.

Que.note: Immutable objects are naturally thread-safe because their state never changes.

Que.q: Q38 : What is the String Pool in Java?
Que.a: The String Pool is a special memory area within the Heap used to store string literals. When a string literal is created, Java first checks whether it already exists in the String Pool. If it does, the existing reference is reused instead of creating a new object. This optimization reduces memory usage and improves performance. Strings created using the new keyword are stored separately in Heap memory. The String Pool is one reason why String objects are immutable in Java.

Que.code:
String s1 = "Java";
String s2 = "Java";

Que.note: String literals with the same value share memory through the String Pool.

Que.q: Q39 : What is a marker interface in Java?
Que.a: A marker interface is an interface that does not contain any methods or constants. It is used to provide metadata or special information to the JVM or framework about a class. Examples include Serializable, Cloneable, and Remote. When a class implements a marker interface, it signals that the class possesses certain capabilities or should receive special treatment. Marker interfaces play an important role in Java APIs and are often used for object serialization, cloning, and distributed computing applications.

Que.q: Q40 : What is cloning in Java?
Que.a: Cloning is the process of creating an exact copy of an existing object in Java. It is achieved using the clone() method and the Cloneable marker interface. Cloning can be shallow or deep depending on how object references are handled. A shallow copy duplicates primitive values and copies references, while a deep copy creates independent copies of referenced objects. Cloning is useful when object duplication is required without manually copying each field. Proper implementation ensures accurate and efficient object replication.

Que.note: Cloning creates a duplicate object without manually copying all fields.

Que.q: Q41 : What is the difference between shallow copy and deep copy in Java?
Que.a: A shallow copy creates a new object but copies references of nested objects instead of creating separate copies. As a result, changes made to referenced objects affect both copies. A deep copy creates a completely independent copy of the object along with all referenced objects. Changes made to one object do not affect the other. Shallow copying is faster and uses less memory, while deep copying provides better isolation and data safety. The choice depends on application requirements and object complexity.

Que.q: Q42 : What is an inner class in Java?
Que.a: An inner class is a class defined inside another class. It has access to all members of the outer class, including private variables and methods. Inner classes are used to logically group classes that are only relevant to the enclosing class and improve code organization. Java supports member inner classes, static nested classes, local inner classes, and anonymous inner classes. They are commonly used in event handling, callbacks, and situations where close association between classes is required.

Que.q: Q43 : What is an anonymous class in Java?
Que.a: An anonymous class is a special type of inner class that does not have a name. It is declared and instantiated in a single expression and is typically used when a class is needed only once. Anonymous classes are often used for event handling, callbacks, and implementing interfaces or abstract classes without creating a separate class file. They help reduce code clutter and improve readability when simple one-time implementations are required within an application.

Que.note: Anonymous classes are commonly used for one-time implementations of interfaces or abstract classes.

Que.q: Q44 : What is the difference between static and non-static methods?
Que.a: Static methods belong to the class itself rather than any specific object and can be called without creating an instance. Non-static methods belong to objects and require an instance of the class for invocation. Static methods can access only static members directly, whereas non-static methods can access both static and instance members. Static methods are commonly used for utility functions, while non-static methods are used when behavior depends on the state of individual objects.

Que.q: Q45 : What is the singleton design pattern in Java?
Que.a: The Singleton design pattern ensures that only one instance of a class exists throughout the application and provides a global access point to that instance. It is commonly used for configuration management, logging services, database connections, and caching mechanisms. The constructor is made private to prevent external object creation, and a static method provides access to the single instance. Singleton helps conserve resources and maintain consistent application behavior when only one shared object is required.

Que.note: Singleton ensures only one object instance exists during application execution.

Que.q: Q46 : What is the difference between fail-fast and fail-safe iterators?
Que.a: Fail-fast and fail-safe iterators differ in how they handle modifications to collections during iteration. Fail-fast iterators immediately throw a ConcurrentModificationException if the collection is modified while being traversed. Examples include iterators from ArrayList and HashMap. Fail-safe iterators work on a copy of the collection and do not throw exceptions when modifications occur. Examples include iterators from CopyOnWriteArrayList. Fail-fast iterators provide error detection, while fail-safe iterators prioritize stability in concurrent environments.

Que.q: Q47 : What is ConcurrentHashMap in Java?
Que.a: ConcurrentHashMap is a thread-safe implementation of the Map interface designed for high-performance concurrent access. Unlike Hashtable, it allows multiple threads to read and write simultaneously without locking the entire map. Internally, it uses advanced locking and synchronization mechanisms to improve scalability and performance. ConcurrentHashMap is commonly used in multithreaded applications where frequent updates and reads occur. It provides better throughput than traditional synchronized collections while maintaining thread safety and data consistency.

Que.q: Q48 : What is an enum in Java?
Que.a: An enum, short for enumeration, is a special data type used to define a fixed set of constants. Enums improve type safety and readability by restricting values to predefined constants. They can contain fields, methods, and constructors, making them more powerful than simple constants. Enums are commonly used for representing days of the week, directions, statuses, and configuration values. Since enums are classes internally, they support object-oriented features while providing a clean way to manage constant values.

Que.note: Enums provide a type-safe way to represent a fixed set of constants.

Que.q: Q49 : What is varargs in Java?
Que.a: Varargs, or variable arguments, allow a method to accept a variable number of arguments of the same type. It simplifies method overloading by enabling developers to pass zero or more values without creating multiple method versions. Internally, varargs are treated as arrays by the compiler. Varargs improve code flexibility and readability when the number of inputs is not fixed. They are widely used in utility methods and APIs where methods need to handle different numbers of arguments dynamically.

Que.q: Q50 : What is autoboxing and unboxing in Java?
Que.a: Autoboxing is the automatic conversion of primitive data types into their corresponding wrapper class objects, while unboxing is the reverse process. For example, converting an int to Integer is autoboxing, and converting Integer back to int is unboxing. These features were introduced to simplify working with collections and generic classes, which require objects instead of primitive types. Autoboxing and unboxing reduce manual conversion code and improve readability while allowing seamless interaction between primitives and wrapper classes.

Que.note: Autoboxing and unboxing automatically convert between primitives and wrapper objects.

Que.q: Q51 : What is Generics in Java?
Que.a: Generics is a feature in Java that enables classes, interfaces, and methods to operate on different data types while providing type safety. It allows developers to specify the type of objects a collection can hold at compile time, reducing runtime errors and eliminating explicit type casting. Generics improve code reusability, readability, and maintainability. They are commonly used with collections such as ArrayList, HashMap, and LinkedList. By enforcing type checking during compilation, generics help create more reliable and robust Java applications.

Que.code: ArrayList<String> names = new ArrayList<String>();

Que.note: Generics provide compile-time type safety and reduce casting.

Que.q: Q52 : What is type erasure in Java?
Que.a: Type erasure is the process by which the Java compiler removes generic type information during compilation and replaces it with appropriate bounds or Object. This ensures backward compatibility with older versions of Java that do not support generics. As a result, generic type information is unavailable at runtime. Although generics improve compile-time safety, the JVM operates on the erased version of the code. Understanding type erasure is important when working with reflection, method overloading, and advanced generic programming techniques.

Que.note: Generic type information exists only at compile time and is removed during compilation.

Que.q: Q53 : What is the difference between List and Set in Java?
Que.a: List and Set are interfaces in the Java Collection Framework used to store groups of objects. A List maintains insertion order and allows duplicate elements. Common implementations include ArrayList and LinkedList. A Set does not allow duplicate elements and may or may not maintain order depending on its implementation. Examples include HashSet and TreeSet. Lists are suitable when duplicates and ordering are important, while Sets are preferred when uniqueness of elements is required.

Que.q: Q54 : What is the difference between HashMap and TreeMap?
Que.a: HashMap and TreeMap are implementations of the Map interface used to store key-value pairs. HashMap stores data using a hash table and does not maintain any order of keys. TreeMap stores entries in sorted order based on keys using a Red-Black Tree. HashMap generally provides faster insertion and retrieval operations, while TreeMap is useful when sorted data is required. The choice depends on whether application requirements prioritize performance or key ordering during data storage and retrieval.

Que.q: Q55 : What is the difference between Comparable and Comparator sorting?
Que.a: Comparable and Comparator are used for sorting objects in Java collections. Comparable defines the natural ordering of objects using the compareTo() method implemented within the class itself. Comparator provides custom sorting logic through the compare() method implemented in a separate class or lambda expression. Comparable supports only one default sorting order, whereas Comparator allows multiple sorting criteria. Developers use Comparable when a single ordering is sufficient and Comparator when flexible or dynamic sorting behavior is required.

Que.note: Comparable provides natural ordering, while Comparator provides custom ordering.

Que.q: Q56 : What is Java 8 and why is it important?
Que.a: Java 8 is one of the most significant releases of Java, introducing powerful features that improved developer productivity and application performance. Major additions include Lambda Expressions, Stream API, Functional Interfaces, Method References, Optional Class, and the new Date and Time API. These features support functional programming concepts and simplify data processing. Java 8 allows developers to write cleaner, more concise, and maintainable code. Due to its stability and feature set, Java 8 remains one of the most widely used Java versions in enterprise applications.

Que.q: Q57 : What is a Lambda Expression in Java?
Que.a: A Lambda Expression is a concise way to represent anonymous functions in Java. Introduced in Java 8, it enables functional programming by allowing methods to be treated as values. Lambda expressions reduce boilerplate code, especially when working with functional interfaces and collections. They are commonly used with the Stream API for filtering, mapping, and processing data. By simplifying code structure and improving readability, lambda expressions make Java applications more expressive and easier to maintain.

Que.code: Runnable r = () -> System.out.println("Hello Java");

Que.note: Lambda expressions provide a compact way to implement functional interfaces.

Que.q: Q58 : What is a Functional Interface in Java?
Que.a: A Functional Interface is an interface that contains exactly one abstract method. It serves as the target type for lambda expressions and method references. Functional interfaces may contain default and static methods in addition to the single abstract method. Java provides several built-in functional interfaces in the java.util.function package, including Predicate, Function, Consumer, and Supplier. Functional interfaces are fundamental to Java's functional programming capabilities introduced in Java 8 and are widely used in modern applications.

Que.q: Q59 : What is Stream API in Java?
Que.a: The Stream API is a feature introduced in Java 8 that allows processing collections of data using a functional programming approach. Streams support operations such as filtering, mapping, sorting, reducing, and collecting data. They help write concise and readable code while improving performance through lazy evaluation and parallel processing capabilities. Stream operations do not modify the original collection but instead produce new results. The API is widely used for efficient data manipulation and transformation in modern Java applications.

Que.note: Streams provide a functional approach to processing collection data.

Que.q: Q60 : What is the difference between map() and flatMap() in Stream API?
Que.a: The map() and flatMap() methods are used to transform data in Java Streams. The map() method transforms each element into another object and returns a stream of transformed elements. The flatMap() method is used when each element may produce multiple results and combines all resulting streams into a single stream. Map creates a one-to-one transformation, whereas flatMap performs one-to-many transformations. FlatMap is commonly used when working with nested collections, arrays, or hierarchical data structures.

Que.q: Q61 : What is Optional class in Java 8?
Que.a: Optional is a container object introduced in Java 8 that may or may not contain a value. It is designed to reduce NullPointerException by providing methods to safely handle null values. Instead of returning null from methods, developers can return an Optional object and use methods such as isPresent(), ifPresent(), orElse(), and orElseGet(). Optional improves code readability and encourages better handling of missing values. It is widely used in modern Java applications and functional programming practices.

Que.code:
Optional<String> name = Optional.of("Java");
System.out.println(name.get());

Que.note: Optional helps avoid NullPointerException and improves code safety.

Que.q: Q62 : What is Method Reference in Java?
Que.a: Method references provide a shorthand syntax for calling methods through lambda expressions. They improve readability by directly referring to existing methods instead of writing explicit lambda expressions. Method references can refer to static methods, instance methods of particular objects, instance methods of arbitrary objects, and constructors. They are commonly used with functional interfaces and Stream API operations. Method references make code cleaner and more maintainable while preserving the benefits of functional programming introduced in Java 8.

Que.code: list.forEach(System.out::println);

Que.q: Q63 : What is Predicate in Java 8?
Que.a: Predicate is a built-in functional interface available in the java.util.function package. It represents a function that accepts one argument and returns a boolean value. Predicates are commonly used for filtering data, validation, and conditional logic within Stream API operations. The interface contains the test() method as its primary abstract method. Additional methods such as and(), or(), and negate() allow combining multiple conditions. Predicates simplify writing reusable and expressive conditional logic in Java applications.

Que.code: Predicate<Integer> isEven = n -> n % 2 == 0;

Que.note: Predicate is used when a condition must return true or false.

Que.q: Q64 : What is Consumer in Java 8?
Que.a: Consumer is a functional interface in the java.util.function package that accepts a single input argument and performs an operation without returning any result. It is commonly used for processing data, logging information, and executing actions on collection elements. The primary method of Consumer is accept(). It can be combined with other consumers using the andThen() method. Consumer is frequently used in Stream API operations such as forEach(), where actions need to be performed on each element.

Que.code: Consumer<String> print = name -> System.out.println(name);

Que.q: Q65 : What is Supplier in Java 8?
Que.a: Supplier is a functional interface that represents a function with no input parameters and a return value. It is commonly used when values need to be generated, provided lazily, or retrieved on demand. The interface contains a single abstract method called get(). Suppliers are useful for object creation, configuration loading, random value generation, and deferred computations. They are widely used in functional programming and Stream API operations where data needs to be supplied dynamically without requiring input arguments.

Que.code: Supplier<String> supplier = () -> "Hello Java";

Que.note: Supplier generates and returns values without accepting any input.

Que.q: Q66 : What is Function interface in Java 8?
Que.a: Function is a functional interface available in the java.util.function package that accepts one argument and produces a result. It is commonly used for transforming data from one form to another. The primary abstract method is apply(), which processes the input and returns an output. Function interfaces are widely used with Stream API operations such as map(). Additional methods like andThen() and compose() allow chaining multiple functions together. Function promotes reusable, concise, and flexible programming practices in Java applications.

Que.code: Function<Integer, String> func = num -> "Number: " + num;

Que.note: Function takes an input and returns a transformed output.

Que.q: Q67 : What is default method in an interface?
Que.a: Default methods were introduced in Java 8 to allow interfaces to contain method implementations. Before Java 8, interfaces could only declare abstract methods. Default methods help add new functionality to existing interfaces without breaking classes that already implement them. They are declared using the default keyword and can be overridden by implementing classes if needed. Default methods support backward compatibility and enable interface evolution while reducing the impact of changes on existing applications and frameworks.

Que.q: Q68 : What is static method in an interface?
Que.a: Static methods in interfaces were introduced in Java 8 and allow interfaces to contain utility methods with implementations. Unlike default methods, static methods belong to the interface itself and cannot be overridden by implementing classes. They are invoked using the interface name rather than an object reference. Static methods improve code organization by keeping related utility functions within the interface. They are commonly used for helper methods, validations, and factory methods associated with interface functionality.

Que.q: Q69 : What is forEach() method in Java 8?
Que.a: The forEach() method is a terminal operation introduced in Java 8 that allows iteration over collection elements using lambda expressions or method references. It simplifies traversal by eliminating the need for traditional loops and iterator objects. The method accepts a Consumer functional interface that defines the action to perform on each element. forEach() improves code readability and integrates seamlessly with Stream API operations. It is commonly used for displaying, processing, or modifying collection data in a concise manner.

Que.code: list.forEach(item -> System.out.println(item));

Que.note: forEach executes a specified action for every element in a collection.

Que.q: Q70 : What is filter() method in Stream API?
Que.a: The filter() method is an intermediate Stream API operation used to select elements that satisfy a specified condition. It accepts a Predicate functional interface and returns a new stream containing only matching elements. Filter operations do not modify the original collection and can be combined with other stream operations such as map(), sorted(), and collect(). Using filter() simplifies data processing and improves code readability by enabling declarative programming. It is one of the most frequently used operations in Java Streams.

Que.note: filter() returns only elements that satisfy the specified condition.

Que.q: Q71 : What is collect() method in Stream API?
Que.a: The collect() method is a terminal operation in the Stream API used to accumulate stream elements into a collection, string, map, or other data structure. It processes all elements of a stream and produces a final result. Common collectors include toList(), toSet(), joining(), groupingBy(), and counting(). The collect() method is widely used because streams themselves do not store data. It enables developers to transform processed stream data into a usable format while maintaining clean and efficient code.

Que.note: collect() converts stream results into collections or other output formats.

Que.q: Q72 : What is reduce() method in Stream API?
Que.a: The reduce() method is a terminal Stream API operation used to combine all elements of a stream into a single result. It repeatedly applies a specified operation to accumulate values. Common use cases include calculating sums, products, maximum values, and custom aggregations. The reduce() method supports functional programming by allowing complex calculations without explicit loops. It improves code readability and integrates seamlessly with other stream operations. Proper use of reduce() can simplify data processing logic significantly.

Que.code:
int sum = numbers.stream()
    .reduce(0, (a, b) -> a + b);

Que.q: Q73 : What is parallel stream in Java?
Que.a: A parallel stream is a type of stream that processes data using multiple threads simultaneously. It leverages the Fork/Join Framework to divide tasks into smaller subtasks and execute them in parallel. Parallel streams can improve performance when working with large datasets and computationally intensive operations. However, they may introduce overhead and should be used carefully when thread safety or ordering requirements exist. Developers can create parallel streams using the parallelStream() method or the parallel() operation on an existing stream.

Que.code:
list.parallelStream()
    .forEach(System.out::println);

Que.note: Parallel streams process data concurrently using multiple threads.

Que.q: Q74 : What is the Fork/Join Framework in Java?
Que.a: The Fork/Join Framework is a parallel execution framework introduced in Java 7 for efficiently utilizing multicore processors. It works by recursively splitting large tasks into smaller subtasks, executing them concurrently, and then combining the results. The framework is based on work-stealing algorithms that improve thread utilization and performance. It is commonly used for divide-and-conquer algorithms, data processing, and parallel computations. The Stream API's parallel processing capabilities are built on top of the Fork/Join Framework.

Que.q: Q75 : What is Executor Framework in Java?
Que.a: The Executor Framework is a high-level concurrency framework that simplifies thread management in Java. Instead of manually creating and controlling threads, developers submit tasks to an ExecutorService, which manages thread creation, scheduling, and execution. The framework improves performance through thread pooling and resource management. Common implementations include FixedThreadPool, CachedThreadPool, and ScheduledThreadPool. The Executor Framework is widely used in enterprise applications because it provides scalable, efficient, and maintainable solutions for concurrent task execution.

Que.note: Executor Framework manages thread execution more efficiently than creating threads manually.

Que.q: Q76 : What is Callable interface in Java?
Que.a: Callable is a functional interface in Java used for tasks that return a result and may throw checked exceptions. Unlike the Runnable interface, which does not return any value, Callable uses the call() method to produce a result. It is commonly used with the Executor Framework and Future interface for asynchronous task execution. Callable improves flexibility in concurrent programming by allowing developers to retrieve task outcomes and handle exceptions effectively while performing background operations.

Que.code: Callable<Integer> task = () -> 100;

Que.note: Callable can return a value and throw checked exceptions.

Que.q: Q77 : What is Future interface in Java?
Que.a: The Future interface represents the result of an asynchronous computation. It is commonly used with the Executor Framework to retrieve results from tasks submitted for execution. Future provides methods such as get(), cancel(), isDone(), and isCancelled() to manage task execution and results. It allows applications to continue processing while a task runs in the background. Future is widely used in multithreaded applications where long-running operations need to be executed asynchronously without blocking the main thread.

Que.code:
Future<Integer> future = executor.submit(() -> 10);
Integer result = future.get();

Que.q: Q78 : What is volatile keyword in Java?
Que.a: The volatile keyword is used to indicate that a variable's value may be modified by multiple threads. It ensures that changes made by one thread are immediately visible to other threads by preventing local thread caching of the variable. Volatile improves visibility but does not provide atomicity or synchronization. It is commonly used for status flags, configuration values, and variables shared between threads. When stronger thread safety guarantees are required, synchronization or concurrent utilities should be used instead.

Que.code: private volatile boolean running = true;

Que.note: Volatile ensures visibility of variable updates across threads.

Que.q: Q79 : What is Java Reflection API?
Que.a: The Reflection API allows Java programs to inspect and manipulate classes, methods, fields, constructors, and annotations at runtime. It enables dynamic behavior by providing access to metadata and class structures without knowing them during compilation. Reflection is commonly used in frameworks, dependency injection containers, testing tools, and object mapping libraries. Although powerful, reflection may impact performance and bypass access restrictions. Developers use it when dynamic loading, runtime inspection, or advanced framework functionality is required.

Que.code:
Class<?> cls = Class.forName("Employee");
System.out.println(cls.getName());

Que.q: Q80 : What is JDBC in Java?
Que.a: JDBC, or Java Database Connectivity, is an API that enables Java applications to interact with relational databases. It provides classes and interfaces for establishing database connections, executing SQL queries, processing results, and managing transactions. JDBC supports multiple database systems through database-specific drivers. The API follows a standard approach, allowing applications to work with different databases with minimal code changes. JDBC is widely used in enterprise applications for data storage, retrieval, reporting, and business transaction processing.

Que.note: JDBC provides a standard way for Java applications to communicate with databases.

Que.q: Q81 : What are JDBC drivers in Java?
Que.a: JDBC drivers are software components that enable Java applications to communicate with databases. They act as a bridge between the JDBC API and the database management system. JDBC drivers translate Java method calls into database-specific commands. Java supports four types of JDBC drivers: JDBC-ODBC Bridge Driver, Native Driver, Network Protocol Driver, and Thin Driver. Modern applications commonly use Type 4 drivers because they are platform-independent, efficient, and communicate directly with the database without requiring additional software.

Que.q: Q82 : What is PreparedStatement in JDBC?
Que.a: PreparedStatement is a JDBC interface used to execute parameterized SQL queries. Unlike Statement, it precompiles SQL queries and allows values to be supplied at runtime through placeholders. This improves performance, reduces parsing overhead, and protects applications from SQL injection attacks. PreparedStatement supports setting parameters using methods such as setInt(), setString(), and setDouble(). It is widely used in enterprise applications because it provides better security, efficiency, and maintainability when interacting with relational databases.

Que.code:
PreparedStatement ps = con.prepareStatement("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id=?");
ps.setInt(1, 101);

Que.note: PreparedStatement helps prevent SQL injection attacks.

Que.q: Q83 : What is the difference between Statement and PreparedStatement?
Que.a: Statement and PreparedStatement are JDBC interfaces used to execute SQL queries. Statement executes static SQL queries and compiles them every time they are executed. PreparedStatement uses precompiled parameterized queries, improving performance and security. Statement is more vulnerable to SQL injection because user input is often concatenated into query strings. PreparedStatement separates SQL code from input values, making applications safer and more efficient. For most database operations involving user input, PreparedStatement is the preferred choice.

Que.q: Q84 : What is ResultSet in JDBC?
Que.a: ResultSet is a JDBC interface that represents the data returned by a database query. It provides methods for navigating through rows and retrieving column values in various data types. ResultSet works like a cursor that points to rows in the query result. Developers can move through records using methods such as next(), previous(), and first(). It supports reading data using methods like getInt(), getString(), and getDate(). ResultSet is a fundamental component of database interaction in Java applications.

Que.q: Q85 : What is transaction management in JDBC?
Que.a: Transaction management in JDBC ensures that a group of database operations is executed as a single unit of work. A transaction follows the ACID principles of Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability. Developers can control transactions using commit() and rollback() methods. If all operations succeed, the transaction is committed; otherwise, it is rolled back to maintain data integrity. Transaction management is essential in banking, e-commerce, and enterprise applications where multiple related database updates must succeed or fail together.

Que.note: Transactions help maintain database consistency and integrity.

Que.q: Q86 : What is ACID property in DBMS and JDBC transactions?
Que.a: ACID is a set of properties that ensure reliable transaction processing in database systems. Atomicity guarantees that all operations in a transaction succeed or fail together. Consistency ensures that data remains valid before and after a transaction. Isolation prevents concurrent transactions from interfering with each other. Durability guarantees that committed changes are permanently stored even after system failures. JDBC transaction management follows ACID principles to maintain data integrity, reliability, and consistency in enterprise applications handling critical business operations.

Que.q: Q87 : What is batch processing in JDBC?
Que.a: Batch processing in JDBC allows multiple SQL statements to be grouped and executed together as a single batch. This reduces database communication overhead and improves performance when handling large numbers of insert, update, or delete operations. Instead of sending queries individually, they are collected and executed in one request. Batch processing is commonly used in data migration, bulk uploads, reporting systems, and enterprise applications. It increases efficiency, minimizes network traffic, and improves overall database interaction performance.

Que.q: Q88 : What is connection pooling in Java?
Que.a: Connection pooling is a technique used to reuse database connections instead of creating a new connection for every request. Since establishing database connections is an expensive operation, pooling improves performance and resource utilization. A pool maintains a collection of open connections that applications can borrow and return when needed. Popular frameworks such as HikariCP, Apache DBCP, and C3P0 provide connection pooling support. It is widely used in enterprise applications to improve scalability, response times, and database efficiency.

Que.note: Connection pooling significantly improves database performance in large applications.

Que.q: Q89 : What is Java NIO?
Que.a: Java NIO, or New Input/Output, is an alternative I/O API introduced to improve performance and scalability compared to traditional Java I/O. NIO uses channels, buffers, selectors, and non-blocking operations to efficiently handle large amounts of data. It is particularly useful in networking and high-performance applications where multiple connections need to be managed simultaneously. By supporting asynchronous and non-blocking communication, Java NIO enables applications to achieve better throughput and resource utilization while processing data.

Que.q: Q90 : What is the difference between Java IO and Java NIO?
Que.a: Java IO and Java NIO are APIs used for input and output operations. Java IO follows a stream-based and blocking approach, where each thread waits until an operation completes. Java NIO uses buffers and channels with support for non-blocking operations, allowing a single thread to manage multiple connections efficiently. NIO generally offers better performance for large-scale and network-intensive applications. While IO is simpler and suitable for basic operations, NIO is preferred for high-performance and scalable systems.

Que.q: Q91 : What is File Handling in Java?
Que.a: File handling in Java refers to the process of creating, reading, writing, updating, and deleting files. Java provides classes such as File, FileReader, FileWriter, BufferedReader, and BufferedWriter to perform file operations efficiently. These classes are available in the java.io package and help applications store and retrieve data from files. File handling is commonly used for logging, configuration management, report generation, and data storage. Proper exception handling is essential during file operations to prevent data loss and runtime errors.

Que.code: File file = new File("data.txt");

Que.note: File handling enables Java applications to interact with files stored on disk.

Que.q: Q92 : What is BufferedReader in Java?
Que.a: BufferedReader is a Java class used to read text efficiently from character input streams. It improves performance by buffering input data and reducing direct interactions with the underlying stream. BufferedReader provides methods such as read(), readLine(), and close() for reading data. It is commonly used with FileReader and InputStreamReader to process text files and console input. By reading larger chunks of data at once, BufferedReader enhances efficiency and reduces the overhead of frequent disk or network access.

Que.code:
BufferedReader br = new BufferedReader(new FileReader("data.txt"));
String line = br.readLine();

Que.q: Q93 : What is BufferedWriter in Java?
Que.a: BufferedWriter is a Java class used to write text efficiently to character output streams. It buffers output data before writing it to the destination, reducing the number of write operations and improving performance. BufferedWriter provides methods such as write(), newLine(), flush(), and close(). It is commonly used with FileWriter to write large amounts of text data to files. By minimizing direct disk access, BufferedWriter helps applications perform output operations more efficiently and reliably.

Que.code:
BufferedWriter bw = new BufferedWriter(new FileWriter("data.txt"));
bw.write("Hello Java");

Que.q: Q94 : What is try-with-resources in Java?
Que.a: Try-with-resources is a feature introduced in Java 7 that automatically closes resources after use. Resources such as files, database connections, and streams must implement the AutoCloseable interface. This feature eliminates the need for explicit finally blocks to close resources and reduces the risk of resource leaks. The syntax is cleaner, easier to maintain, and less error-prone. Try-with-resources is considered a best practice for managing resources because it ensures proper cleanup even when exceptions occur during execution.

Que.note: Resources declared in try-with-resources are automatically closed.

Que.q: Q95 : What is AutoCloseable interface in Java?
Que.a: AutoCloseable is an interface introduced in Java 7 that allows resources to be automatically closed when they are no longer needed. Classes implementing this interface provide a close() method that is invoked automatically by the try-with-resources statement. Many Java classes such as streams, readers, writers, and database connections implement AutoCloseable. Using this interface improves resource management, reduces memory leaks, and ensures proper cleanup of system resources. It is an important part of modern Java programming practices.

Que.q: Q96 : What is Java Annotation?
Que.a: Annotations are metadata added to Java code that provide information to the compiler, JVM, or frameworks. They do not directly affect program execution but influence how code is processed. Java provides built-in annotations such as @Override, @Deprecated, and @SuppressWarnings. Developers can also create custom annotations for specific requirements. Annotations are widely used in frameworks like Spring, Hibernate, and JUnit for configuration, dependency injection, validation, and testing. They help reduce configuration complexity and improve code readability and maintainability.

Que.note: Annotations provide metadata about code without changing business logic.

Que.q: Q97 : What is @Override annotation in Java?
Que.a: The @Override annotation indicates that a method is intended to override a method from its superclass or implemented interface. It helps the compiler verify that the method signature is correct and prevents mistakes caused by incorrect method names or parameters. If the method does not actually override a parent method, the compiler generates an error. Using @Override improves code readability, maintainability, and reliability. It is considered a best practice whenever method overriding is performed in Java applications.

Que.q: Q98 : What is @Deprecated annotation in Java?
Que.a: The @Deprecated annotation is used to indicate that a class, method, field, or constructor should no longer be used because a better alternative exists. When developers use deprecated elements, the compiler generates warnings to encourage migration to newer implementations. Deprecation helps maintain backward compatibility while guiding developers toward improved APIs. It is commonly used when features become outdated, insecure, or inefficient. Proper documentation often accompanies deprecated elements to explain replacement options and migration strategies.

Que.note: Deprecated elements should be avoided in new development whenever possible.

Que.q: Q99 : What is EnumSet in Java?
Que.a: EnumSet is a specialized Set implementation designed specifically for enum types. It is highly optimized and uses bit vectors internally, making it more efficient than general-purpose set implementations. EnumSet stores only enum constants of a single enum type and provides fast operations such as add, remove, and contains. It maintains the natural order of enum constants and consumes less memory. EnumSet is commonly used when working with groups of related enum values in Java applications.

Que.code: EnumSet<Day> days = EnumSet.of(Day.MONDAY, Day.FRIDAY);

Que.q: Q100 : What is EnumMap in Java?
Que.a: EnumMap is a specialized Map implementation designed for use with enum keys. It stores key-value pairs where all keys belong to a single enum type. EnumMap is highly efficient because it uses arrays internally rather than hash tables. It provides faster performance and lower memory consumption compared to HashMap when enum keys are involved. EnumMap maintains the natural order of enum constants and is commonly used in applications where enum values are associated with specific configurations, states, or business rules.

Que.code: EnumMap<Day, String> schedule = new EnumMap<>(Day.class);

Que.note: EnumMap is optimized for storing values against enum keys.

Que.q: Q101 : What is Java Memory Model (JMM)?
Que.a: The Java Memory Model defines how threads interact with memory and how changes made by one thread become visible to other threads. It establishes rules for reading and writing shared variables in multithreaded applications. JMM ensures consistency and predictability by defining concepts such as visibility, atomicity, and ordering. Keywords like volatile, synchronized, and final play important roles within the memory model. Understanding JMM is essential for writing correct concurrent programs and avoiding issues such as race conditions and stale data.

Que.q: Q102 : What is race condition in Java?
Que.a: A race condition occurs when multiple threads access and modify shared data simultaneously without proper synchronization. The final outcome depends on the order and timing of thread execution, which can lead to inconsistent or unexpected results. Race conditions are common in multithreaded applications where shared resources are updated concurrently. They can be prevented using synchronization, locks, atomic classes, or concurrent collections. Identifying and eliminating race conditions is important for ensuring data integrity and application reliability.

Que.code:
Thread A increments count
Thread B increments count
Result may be inconsistent

Que.note: Race conditions occur due to unsynchronized access to shared resources.

Que.q: Q103 : What is AtomicInteger in Java?
Que.a: AtomicInteger is a class from the java.util.concurrent.atomic package that provides atomic operations on integer values. It allows thread-safe updates without using synchronized blocks or locks. Methods such as incrementAndGet(), decrementAndGet(), and compareAndSet() ensure atomic execution of operations. AtomicInteger improves performance in concurrent applications by reducing locking overhead. It is commonly used for counters, sequence generators, and shared numeric values where thread-safe updates are required without the complexity of traditional synchronization mechanisms.

Que.code:
AtomicInteger counter = new AtomicInteger(0);
counter.incrementAndGet();

Que.q: Q104 : What is ExecutorService in Java?
Que.a: ExecutorService is an interface in the Executor Framework that manages thread execution and lifecycle. It provides methods for submitting tasks, shutting down executors, and handling asynchronous operations. ExecutorService simplifies multithreading by abstracting thread creation and management. It supports task execution using Runnable and Callable interfaces and can return results through Future objects. Common implementations include fixed thread pools, cached thread pools, and scheduled thread pools. It is widely used in enterprise applications for scalable concurrent processing.

Que.code:
ExecutorService service = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(5);
service.submit(() -> System.out.println("Task Running"));

Que.q: Q105 : What is CountDownLatch in Java?
Que.a: CountDownLatch is a synchronization utility that allows one or more threads to wait until a set of operations performed by other threads completes. It is initialized with a count value, and each completed task decrements the count using countDown(). Waiting threads call await() and remain blocked until the count reaches zero. CountDownLatch is useful for coordinating thread execution, waiting for service initialization, and ensuring that multiple tasks finish before proceeding with the next step in a workflow.

Que.note: CountDownLatch helps coordinate multiple threads and task completion.

Que.q: Q106 : What is CyclicBarrier in Java?
Que.a: CyclicBarrier is a synchronization utility that allows a group of threads to wait for each other at a common execution point. Once the specified number of threads reaches the barrier, all waiting threads are released simultaneously. Unlike CountDownLatch, CyclicBarrier can be reused after the waiting threads are released. It is commonly used in parallel computations, simulations, and multi-stage processing tasks where multiple threads must complete a phase before proceeding to the next stage. This utility improves coordination among concurrent tasks.

Que.code:
CyclicBarrier barrier = new CyclicBarrier(3);
barrier.await();

Que.note: CyclicBarrier can be reused multiple times after all threads reach the barrier.

Que.q: Q107 : What is Semaphore in Java?
Que.a: Semaphore is a synchronization utility that controls access to a shared resource by maintaining a set number of permits. Threads must acquire a permit before accessing the resource and release it after use. If no permits are available, threads wait until one becomes available. Semaphores are commonly used for connection pools, rate limiting, resource management, and controlling concurrent access. They help prevent resource exhaustion and ensure efficient utilization of limited resources in multithreaded applications.

Que.q: Q108 : What is ReentrantLock in Java?
Que.a: ReentrantLock is a locking mechanism provided by the java.util.concurrent.locks package. It offers more flexibility than the synchronized keyword by supporting features such as fairness policies, interruptible locks, timed lock attempts, and multiple condition variables. A thread that already owns the lock can acquire it again without causing deadlock, which is why it is called reentrant. ReentrantLock is commonly used in advanced concurrency scenarios where greater control over thread synchronization and locking behavior is required.

Que.note: ReentrantLock provides advanced locking features beyond synchronized blocks.

Que.q: Q109 : What is BlockingQueue in Java?
Que.a: BlockingQueue is an interface in the Java Collections Framework designed for producer-consumer scenarios. It supports operations that wait automatically when the queue is empty during retrieval or full during insertion. This eliminates the need for explicit synchronization in many concurrent applications. Common implementations include ArrayBlockingQueue, LinkedBlockingQueue, and PriorityBlockingQueue. BlockingQueue is widely used in thread pools, messaging systems, task scheduling, and asynchronous processing where safe communication between producer and consumer threads is required.

Que.q: Q110 : What is CompletableFuture in Java?
Que.a: CompletableFuture is an advanced asynchronous programming class introduced in Java 8. It extends the capabilities of the Future interface by allowing non-blocking task execution, result transformation, task chaining, and exception handling. Developers can combine multiple asynchronous operations and define actions that execute automatically when tasks complete. CompletableFuture improves responsiveness and scalability in modern applications by reducing thread blocking. It is commonly used in web services, microservices, and applications that require efficient asynchronous processing.

Que.code:
CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> "Hello")
    .thenAccept(System.out::println);

Que.note: CompletableFuture supports asynchronous workflows and task chaining.

Que.q: Q111 : What is Java 9 Module System?
Que.a: The Java Module System, introduced in Java 9, provides a way to organize applications into independent modules. A module is a collection of related packages and resources with a defined interface. Modules improve maintainability, security, and performance by allowing developers to explicitly declare dependencies and control access to internal components. The module system reduces classpath issues and supports scalable application development. It is particularly useful for large enterprise applications where code organization and dependency management are important concerns.

Que.note: Modules improve application organization and dependency management.

Que.q: Q112 : What is Stream API lazy evaluation?
Que.a: Lazy evaluation is a key feature of the Java Stream API where intermediate operations are not executed immediately. Instead, they are stored and executed only when a terminal operation such as collect(), forEach(), or reduce() is invoked. This approach improves performance by avoiding unnecessary computations and processing only the required elements. Lazy evaluation enables operation chaining and optimization within streams. It helps developers write efficient and concise code while minimizing resource consumption during data processing tasks.

Que.q: Q113 : What is Java Record?
Que.a: Records were introduced in Java to simplify the creation of immutable data carrier classes. A record automatically generates common methods such as constructors, getters, equals(), hashCode(), and toString(). This reduces boilerplate code and improves readability. Records are ideal for representing data objects where the primary purpose is storing and transferring information. Since records are immutable by default, they provide thread safety and predictable behavior. They are widely used in modern Java applications for DTOs and configuration objects.

Que.code: public record Employee(int id, String name) {}

Que.q: Q114 : What is sealed class in Java?
Que.a: Sealed classes are a feature introduced in modern Java that allow developers to control which classes can extend or implement a particular class or interface. By explicitly listing permitted subclasses, sealed classes improve security, maintainability, and predictability of inheritance hierarchies. They are useful when only a limited set of implementations should exist. Sealed classes work together with final and non-sealed modifiers to provide flexible inheritance control. This feature enhances domain modeling and reduces unintended class extensions.

Que.code: public sealed class Shape permits Circle, Rectangle {}

Que.note: Sealed classes restrict inheritance to explicitly permitted subclasses.

Que.q: Q115 : What is the difference between final, finally, and finalize()?
Que.a: Final, finally, and finalize() are different concepts in Java. The final keyword is used to restrict modification of variables, methods, and classes. The finally block is part of exception handling and executes regardless of whether an exception occurs. The finalize() method was historically used by the garbage collector before object destruction, though it is now deprecated and should be avoided. Understanding these differences is important because they serve completely different purposes despite having similar names.

Que.q: Q116 : What is Object class in Java?
Que.a: The Object class is the root class of the Java class hierarchy. Every class in Java directly or indirectly inherits from the Object class. It provides common methods such as equals(), hashCode(), toString(), getClass(), clone(), and wait(). These methods enable object comparison, string representation, synchronization, and runtime information retrieval. Since all Java objects inherit from Object, its methods are available throughout the language. Understanding the Object class is essential because it forms the foundation of Java's object-oriented programming model.

Que.q: Q117 : Why do we override hashCode() and equals() together?
Que.a: The equals() method determines logical equality between objects, while hashCode() generates a numeric value used in hash-based collections such as HashMap and HashSet. If two objects are considered equal by equals(), they must return the same hash code. Failing to override both methods consistently can cause unexpected behavior in collections, such as duplicate entries or failed lookups. Overriding them together ensures correct object comparison, proper hashing behavior, and reliable performance when objects are stored in hash-based data structures.

Que.note: Equal objects must always return the same hash code.

Que.q: Q118 : What is the contract between equals() and hashCode()?
Que.a: The contract between equals() and hashCode() states that if two objects are equal according to the equals() method, they must return the same hash code value. However, objects with the same hash code are not necessarily equal. Consistency between these methods is crucial for the correct functioning of hash-based collections. Violating this contract can lead to unpredictable behavior during insertion, retrieval, and deletion operations. Java developers must ensure that both methods are implemented together whenever logical equality is customized.

Que.q: Q119 : What is String immutability in Java?
Que.a: String immutability means that once a String object is created, its value cannot be changed. Any operation that appears to modify a string actually creates a new String object. Immutability improves security, thread safety, caching, and performance through the String Pool mechanism. Since strings are widely used for file paths, network connections, database queries, and security-sensitive information, immutability prevents accidental modifications. This design decision is one of the reasons why String is considered a special and highly optimized class in Java.

Que.code:
String s = "Java";
s.concat(" Programming");

Que.note: The original String object remains unchanged after modification operations.

Que.q: Q120 : Why is String immutable in Java?
Que.a: String is immutable in Java to improve security, performance, thread safety, and memory optimization. Immutable strings can be safely shared between multiple threads without synchronization. They support the String Pool, which reduces memory usage by reusing identical string literals. Immutability also prevents accidental modification of sensitive values such as file paths, URLs, usernames, and database connection strings. Because String objects cannot change after creation, Java can optimize storage and execution while maintaining predictable and reliable application behavior.

Que.q: Q121 : What is ClassLoader in Java?
Que.a: ClassLoader is a subsystem of the JVM responsible for loading class files into memory when they are required during program execution. It dynamically loads classes and prevents all classes from being loaded at startup, improving performance and memory utilization. Java follows a hierarchical class loading mechanism consisting of Bootstrap, Extension, and Application ClassLoaders. ClassLoader ensures that classes are loaded only once and provides security by controlling how classes enter the JVM. It is a fundamental part of Java's runtime architecture.

Que.q: Q122 : What is the difference between ClassNotFoundException and NoClassDefFoundError?
